title: A Tamil Immigrant on a Student Visa Just Won a Seat in the Scottish Parliament. Now the Real Fight Begins.
excerpt: Q Manivannan's election as an MSP has ignited a fierce debate over immigration, political eligibility, and what it means to belong — and NRIs worldwide recognise the story all too well.
body:
Q Manivannan does not fit neatly into any box — which is precisely the point.

The 30-something anthropologist from Tamil Nadu, who identifies as non-binary and transgender, was elected to the Scottish Parliament on May 7 as a Member of the Scottish Parliament (MSP) for the Edinburgh and Lothians East region, running on the Scottish Greens’ regional list. The victory made Manivannan the first person elected to Holyrood on a student visa — a milestone enabled by a 2025 law change that allowed foreign nationals with valid visas, even temporary ones, to stand for office in Scotland.

The reaction was immediate and polarised.

## A Rule Change That Changed Everything

Until recently, standing for the Scottish Parliament required either British citizenship or indefinite leave to remain in the UK. The SNP government’s legislative change opened the door to anyone with a lawful right to reside — including those on student or graduate visas. It was a quiet reform that attracted little attention until Manivannan’s candidacy made it impossible to ignore.

Manivannan, who has lived in Scotland since 2021 and holds a PhD, ran on a platform of “kinder politics” rooted in care for working-class and marginalised communities. The campaign raised £1,600 through crowdfunding. The Scottish Greens, who recorded their best-ever election result, called Manivannan “a politician of care.”

But for critics, the election exposed what they see as a dangerous loophole. Scottish Conservative MSP Tim Eagle said voters would be “astonished” that someone on a student visa could hold public office. An SNP veteran publicly called on the Greens to withdraw Manivannan. And Reform UK’s Scottish leader, Lord Malcolm Offord, accused the Greens of putting Manivannan’s immigration status “at risk” by encouraging them to stand.

## The Visa Clock

The most immediate question is practical: can Manivannan actually serve a full five-year term?

Scottish Greens co-leader Gillian Mackay acknowledged that Manivannan would need to secure a new visa — first a graduate route visa (costing £2,089), then potentially a global talent visa (£5,047). Manivannan reportedly pleaded with colleagues for financial help to cover the costs.

Mackay said she believed it was “likely” the visa would be granted, but conceded the risk. “There will have to be a renewal of Q’s visa,” she told the BBC. “Anything that we can do to support Q through that, we will.”

The Home Office has been urged by Scottish Conservatives to investigate whether Manivannan’s role as an MSP — a full-time, salaried position — violates student visa conditions that typically cap work at 20 hours per week. The Greens argue the Parliament specifically legislated to permit this, and that Manivannan holds a valid visa with the right to work.

## What NRIs See in This Story

For Indians in the diaspora, the Q Manivannan saga touches something deeper than Scottish electoral law.

The story of an Indian-origin immigrant navigating hostile visa systems, facing questions about belonging, and being told — sometimes explicitly — that they don’t have the right credentials to participate in public life is achingly familiar. Across the US, UK, Canada, and Australia, NRIs routinely encounter the gap between being economically essential and politically invisible.

In the UK specifically, the hostile environment policy has made visa renewals a source of chronic anxiety for hundreds of thousands of South Asian immigrants. The cost of extending a visa, applying for indefinite leave to remain, or sponsoring family members has become prohibitive — a system that critics say prices out all but the wealthiest immigrants from full participation in British life.

Manivannan’s election is, depending on who you ask, either a triumph of inclusive democracy or a cautionary tale about lowering barriers too far. But for NRIs who have spent years — sometimes decades — navigating visa bureaucracies while building lives in countries they may never fully “belong” to, the resonance is unmistakable.

## The Controversy That Won’t Quiet Down

The backlash has extended beyond visa questions. Reports surfaced that Manivannan had bragged about “unfollowing” the Auschwitz Memorial on social media and expressed support for the vandalism of posters of Israeli hostages. The Scottish Greens said the unfollowing was a response to statements by the memorial that were viewed as downplaying suffering in Gaza, but the controversy has provided ammunition to opponents from across the political spectrum.

Reform UK’s Thomas Kerr argued that the antisemitism allegations were more disqualifying than Manivannan’s immigration status. “The reason he shouldn’t be in parliament is nothing to do with where he has come from,” Kerr said.

Meanwhile, legal experts have raised the possibility that Manivannan could theoretically serve out the parliamentary term “in exile” — continuing to vote and participate remotely if forced to leave the UK. Constitutional scholar Alistair Clark warned this scenario, while legally possible, could damage Holyrood’s reputation.

## What Happens Next

The immediate future hinges on Manivannan’s visa renewal. If the Home Office grants a graduate visa — and subsequently a global talent visa — the MSP could serve the full term with relative security. If not, the Scottish Greens would face the politically excruciating prospect of losing a seat they won fairly under rules they championed.

For the broader Indian diaspora, the story is a reminder that political representation remains contested terrain. In the same month that Q Manivannan took their oath at Holyrood, Indian-origin politicians across the Western world continue to navigate the tension between being celebrated as success stories and being interrogated about their right to be there.

The student visa will expire. The debate won’t.
author: Diaspora Desk
